g.text: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as automated
evaluators—a paradigm known as LLM-as-a-Judge (Zheng et al., 2023)—to assess
the quality of model-generated text at scale.
g.title: N1 [Context] (cites=1) Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as automated evaluators—a paradigm known as LLM-as-a-Judge (Zheng et al., 2023)—to assess the quality of model-generated text at scale.

g.text: This approach has enabled benchmarks such as MT-Bench (Zheng et al., 2023),
G-Eval (Liu et al., 2023), and LiveMedBench (Yan et al., 2026) to evaluate
open-ended responses without requiring expensive human annotation.
g.title: N2 [Context] (cites=3) This approach has enabled benchmarks such as MT-Bench (Zheng et al., 2023), G-Eval (Liu et al., 2023), and LiveMedBench (Yan et al., 2026) to evaluate open-ended responses without requiring expensive human annotation.

g.text: LLM judges vulnerable to prompt injection
However, recent work has raised concerns about the vulnerability of LLM
judges to prompt injection attacks, where adversarial content embedded in
evaluated responses manipulates the judge's output (Maloyan et al., 2025;
g.title: N3 [Context] (cites=2) However, recent work has raised concerns about the vulnerability of LLM judges to prompt injection attacks, where adversarial content embedded in evaluated responses manipulates the judge's output (Maloyan et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2025).

g.text: LiveMedBench presents a particularly interesting case study for security
g.title: N4 [Prior_Work] (cites=0) LiveMedBench presents a particularly interesting case study for security analysis.

g.text: Its rubric grader directly interpolates model responses into the judge
prompt without explicit untrusted-data framing, and employs permissive
fallback parsing that searches for substrings like "met" and true when JSON
g.title: N5 [Prior_Work] (cites=0) Its rubric grader directly interpolates model responses into the judge prompt without explicit untrusted-data framing, and employs permissive fallback parsing that searches for substrings like "met" and true when JSON parsing fails.

g.text: These design choices create theoretical attack surfaces: an adversary could
inject instructions to override the judge's evaluation logic or craft
responses that trigger favorable fallback parsing.
g.title: N6 [Limitation] (cites=0) These design choices create theoretical attack surfaces: an adversary could inject instructions to override the judge's evaluation logic or craft responses that trigger favorable fallback parsing.

g.text: In our experiments, 99.78% of baseline evaluations triggered these
g.title: N7 [Result] (cites=0) In our experiments, 99.78% of baseline evaluations triggered these fallback heuristics.

g.text: We conduct the first security audit of LiveMedBench's rubric grader, testing
three injection payload families (direct override, format spoofing, and
fallback-parse trigger) and implementing a four-layer hardening strategy
g.title: N8 [Method] (cites=0) We conduct the first security audit of LiveMedBench's rubric grader, testing three injection payload families (direct override, format spoofing, and fallback-parse trigger) and implementing a four-layer hardening strategy (untrusted data framing, schema-constrained output, strict parsing, and evidence verification).

g.text: Negative: robust baseline; -6.42% drift from hardening
Our findings constitute a negative result: the baseline grader
demonstrates natural robustness to all tested attacks, while the
hardening introduces a statistically significant benign drift of
g.title: N9 [Result] (cites=0) Our findings constitute a negative result: the baseline grader demonstrates natural robustness to all tested attacks, while the hardening introduces a statistically significant benign drift of −6.42% without providing measurable security benefit.

g.text: First, we present the first security audit of
LiveMedBench's rubric grader against prompt injection
attacks, testing three payload families targeting
g.title: C1 [Contribution] (cites=0) First, we present the first security audit of LiveMedBench's rubric grader against prompt injection attacks, testing three payload families targeting distinct attack vectors.

g.text: Second, we provide empirical evidence that the baseline
grader is naturally robust to the tested attacks, with
g.title: C2 [Contribution] (cites=0) Second, we provide empirical evidence that the baseline grader is naturally robust to the tested attacks, with no statistically significant score inflation (all 95% CIs include zero).

g.text: Third, we demonstrate that a four-layer hardening
strategy causes net harm: −6.42% benign drift (CI
g.title: C3 [Contribution] (cites=0) Third, we demonstrate that a four-layer hardening strategy causes net harm: −6.42% benign drift (CI excludes zero) without security improvement.

g.text: Fourth, we recommend that security interventions in LLM
evaluation pipelines be empirically validated on both
adversarial and benign conditions before deployment.
g.title: C4 [Contribution] (cites=0) Fourth, we recommend that security interventions in LLM evaluation pipelines be empirically validated on both adversarial and benign conditions before deployment.
